title: Credential Stuffing: Detection and Response
summary: Distinguishing credential stuffing from brute force and responding to account takeover.
content:
# Credential Stuffing: Detection and Response

## What it is
Credential stuffing replays username and password pairs stolen from an unrelated breach
against your login endpoint, betting on password reuse. It differs from brute force in an
important way: each individual attempt uses a plausible, previously valid password, so the
per-account failure count stays low and lockout thresholds are never reached. Success rates
are small in percentage terms but large in absolute terms against a big user base.

## Detection
The signal is distributional rather than per-account. Look for a spike in overall login
volume with an unusually low success rate; attempts spread across many distinct accounts with
one or two tries each; a large number of source addresses each making few attempts, often via
residential proxy networks; and repeated identical User-Agent strings or TLS fingerprints
across otherwise unrelated addresses.

Successful logins from addresses, devices or geographies never previously seen for that
account are the outcome to alert on. A sudden rise in password-reset requests can indicate
users discovering compromised accounts.

## Triage
Establish the size of the successful set, not just the attempt volume. For each compromised
account, determine what was accessed and whether any secondary action followed - email
address change, MFA enrolment change, payment detail update, data export. Those follow-on
actions distinguish an opportunistic login from an active takeover.

## Containment
Force a password reset on every confirmed compromised account and invalidate its sessions.
Where the compromised account changed its own recovery details, restore them and treat the
account as fully attacker-controlled until the legitimate owner is verified out of band.
Rate-limit the login endpoint by source and introduce a challenge for anomalous attempts.

## Prevention
Require MFA, which defeats stuffing almost entirely. Check submitted passwords against known
breach corpora at registration and reset. Rate-limit and challenge by source address and
device fingerprint rather than by account alone, since per-account limits do not see this
attack. Alert users to logins from new devices.
